text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London jumped in late afternoon trade fuelled by New York's steep rise on a report, later said to have been based on an erroneous calculation, the Colombian National Coffee Growers' Federation cut its 1996/97 crop estimates to 8.3 million bags, from 10.4 million bags forecast previously. By the close the London May robusta contract was $35 firmer at $1,580 per tonne. Arabica futures in New York ended up sharply in volatile trading, but prices came reeling off highs after Colombia reiterated that its previous forecast of 10.4 million bags still stands.

Most active May coffee bounded to a fresh life of contract high of 177 cents/lb on the bullish Colombian estimate, before closing at 172.85 cents, up 9.60 cents on the day. Spot March surged 11.30 cents to 185.45 cents, a two-year high on the continuous weekly chart, but off its new contract high of 189.00 cents. The nearby March/May switch, a barometer of near term availability ballooned to 12.60 cents, up from 10.90 cents the previous day. May/July widened to 8.60 cents from 6.90 cents the previous session.

COLOMBIA - A spokesman for Colombia's National Coffee Growers' Federation said the forecast of 8.3 million 60-kg bags for the 1996/97 coffee year was based on an erroneous calculation and reiterated the previous forecast of 10.4 million bags. According to Roman Medina, the calculation had failed to take into account 2 million bags of coffee produced in January, February and March. He said production for the coffee year was still seen at a level of about 10.4 million bags, down from 12.9 million bags in 1995/96. In the meantime it was reported that the Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange (CSCE) planned to look into the circumstances surrounding the erroneous report from Colombia. The exchange said it would ask the Commodity Futures Trading Commission to work with them on the matter.

UNITED STATES - US certified coffee stocks rose by 2,000 bags on February 25 to 26,045 bags (24,045 bags). While stocks in Miami and San Francisco remained unchanged, stocks in New Orleans rose to 9,501 bags (8,001 bags) and stocks in New York rose to 1,025 bags (525 bags).

ITALY - Coffee imports in September 1996 amounted to 511,530 60-kg bags, up from last year's 464,579 bags. This brought cumulative imports in the first three quarters of 1996 (January/September) up to 4.219 million bags, 4.6 per cent up on the tonnage imported in the like period the previous year. Total imports in calendar year 1995 amounted to 5.387 million bags compared to 5.474 million bags in 1994. Major suppliers of green coffee in January/September 1996 were Brazil (903,200 vs 1.088 million bags), Zaire (375,200 vs 538,100 bags), India (343,300 vs 290,200 bags) and Ivory Coast (339,200 vs 343,200 bags).

Coffee exports in September 1996 reached 65,375 bags, slightly up on last year's 63,274 bags. This brought cumulative exports in January/September 1996 up to 589,507 bags, 14.5 per cent up on exports in January/September 1995. Total exports in 1995 reached 738,894 bags compared to 702,542 bags in 1994. Italy exports most of its coffee in the form of roast and grounds with France (221,900 vs 185,200 bags), Germany (96,200 vs 71,300 bags) and the US (32,600 vs 25,700 bags) being the main markets.
